articles.title: ForageQuest: A Single-File AI That Tells You Not to Eat the Mushroom
articles.excerpt: I love foraging. I also love not dying. Those two things are in tension when you're holding a mushroom with no signal and no idea if it's a chanterelle or a jack o'lantern. Every foraging app wanted a…
articles.body: I love foraging. I also love not dying. Those two things are in tension when you're holding a mushroom with no signal and no idea if it's a chanterelle or a jack o'lantern. Every foraging app wanted a server, an API key, and a monthly fee. That's backwards. On a trail, a cloud app is useless exactly when you need it most. So I built ForageQuest - a gamified foraging companion that runs an open-weight vision model entirely in your browser. One HTML file. No backend. No API keys. No data leaves your device. And the part I'm proudest of: it knows when it doesn't know. Why open matters here Offline safety. Trails have no signal. CLIP runs on WebGPU in your browser, cached after first load. Zero bars, still works. Privacy. Your foraging spots are your secret.

articles.title: S3 Object Lambda for AI: Transforming Images on the Fly for Claude Vision, Explained Simply
articles.excerpt: Developers often copy images from S3 to a server just to resize them before sending them to a LLM’s vision model. What if the transformation could happen inside S3, eliminating the extra hop? This pos…
articles.body: Developers often copy images from S3 to a server just to resize them before sending them to a LLM’s vision model. What if the transformation could happen inside S3, eliminating the extra hop? This post shows how to let Claude’s Vision API see resized images without any custom compute. Why Object Lambda matters for AI workloads When an AI service asks for an image, the usual pattern looks like this: A backend pulls the original file from an S3 bucket. The backend runs a resizing library (Sharp, Pillow, etc.). The resized bytes travel over the network again, this time to the AI endpoint. Each step adds latency, CPU usage, and a point of failure. Object Lambda changes the story by letting you attach a tiny piece of code (a transform function ) directly to an S3 access point .

articles.title: A failed build un-bumps our version and a failed upload does not, and one line is the difference
articles.excerpt: pnpm release does three things in order: bumps the version in app/package.json, builds the installers with electron-builder, and uploads them to Cloudflare R2. One command, about 500 lines of Node, no…
articles.body: pnpm release does three things in order: bumps the version in app/package.json , builds the installers with electron-builder, and uploads them to Cloudflare R2. One command, about 500 lines of Node, no CI involved, because the Mac installer can only be built on a Mac and the Windows one only on Windows. Most of that script is uninteresting. Four decisions in it are not, and all four are about refusing to do something. The bump has to survive a failed upload and not a failed build A version bump is a file edit that happens before the thing it describes exists. If the build then fails, package.json claims a version that was never produced. So the script registers an exit hook: let revertOnExit = bumped ; process .

articles.title: What AI agents actually do with your MCP server
articles.excerpt: An MCP server can look healthy in every log and still be hard for agents to use. Requests come in, responses go out, nothing crashes. What you don't see is how the agent got there: what it asked for t…
articles.body: An MCP server can look healthy in every log and still be hard for agents to use. Requests come in, responses go out, nothing crashes. What you don't see is how the agent got there: what it asked for that you don't have, what it got wrong before it got it right, and where it got stuck. These are the five things that only showed up once I measured them. The screenshots are from a demo flight-booking server with simulated traffic, so the numbers are examples; the patterns are the ones agents produce. 1. Agents call tools you don't have Agents guess tool names. Some guesses are near misses: searchFlights when the tool is search_flights , seatMap instead of seat_map . Others are a tool the agent assumed should exist, like get_flight_price .

articles.title: PDF to markdown for LLMs
articles.excerpt: Converting a PDF to markdown for an LLM means turning pages into text that keeps the structure a model needs: headings as headings, tables as tables, columns in reading order. Markdown is the usual ta…
articles.body: Converting a PDF to markdown for an LLM means turning pages into text that keeps the structure a model needs: headings as headings, tables as tables, columns in reading order. Markdown is the usual target because models read it well, it is usually lighter than HTML, and a RAG pipeline can split it on headings instead of on arbitrary character counts. You do this for one of three reasons: to index documents for retrieval, to paste a document into a prompt without losing its tables, or to give an agent a file it can read. Plain text extraction is not enough for any of the three, because a table flattened into one cell per line is worse than no table. This page runs three open-source converters on the same PDFs, shows the code, and reports what came out.
